Course.title: Calculus I (Bio. & Soc. Sci.)
Course.assumed_background: Precalculus: basic properties of functions, exponential growth and decay, and sequences (reviewed in the opening unit)

Module.title: Review Basic Properties of Functions
Module.goal: Reinforce the precalculus toolkit — function properties, exponential growth and decay, and sequences — that the rest of the course builds on.

Module.title: Limits and Continuity
Module.goal: Develop the limit concept, including formal definitions, and use it to characterize continuity and limits at infinity.

Module.title: Derivatives
Module.goal: Introduce the derivative from its formal definition and build fluency with the full set of differentiation rules.

Module.title: Applications of Differentiation
Module.goal: Apply derivatives to analyze function behavior, solve optimization problems, and evaluate limits via L'Hôpital's Rule.

Module.title: Integration
Module.goal: Define the definite integral, establish the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and apply integration to concrete problems.

Module.title: Applications of the Integral
Module.goal: Extend integration technique with substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions to handle a wider class of integrals.

Concept.name: Basic Properties of Functions
Concept.summary: Core precalculus facts about functions — domain, range, composition, inverses, and the standard families (polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric) — reviewed so later limit and derivative work has a reliable foundation.
key_definitions: Function: a rule assigning to each input in its domain exactly one output
Domain and range of a function
Composition of functions and inverse functions
Linear, polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric function families

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat domain restrictions as optional bookkeeping and evaluate composed or inverse functions outside their valid domains.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require explicit domain/range statements on every worked example and have students verify composition and inverse identities on restricted domains.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students conflate inverse functions with reciprocals (f^{-1}(x) vs. 1/f(x)).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast the two notations side by side and check inverses by composing to the identity.

Concept.name: Exponential Growth and Decay
Concept.summary: Exponential models of the form N(t) = N0 e^{rt} (or N0 a^t), including doubling time, half-life, and the biological and social-science interpretations of the growth/decay constant.
key_definitions: Exponential growth/decay function N(t) = N0 e^{rt}
Growth rate r and base a
Doubling time and half-life

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students read the growth rate r as a percentage per time step rather than as the continuous rate in e^{rt}, and mis-handle unit conversions.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Work paired examples converting between a^t and e^{rt} forms and between doubling time and r.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply exponential models outside their valid regime (e.g., unbounded growth in a resource-limited population).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Discuss model assumptions and short biological/social examples where exponential growth is only locally valid.

Concept.name: Sequences
Concept.summary: Sequences as functions on the natural numbers, including recursive and closed-form descriptions, arithmetic and geometric sequences, and the idea of a sequence limit that previews the limit concept.
key_definitions: Sequence as a function a_n on the natural numbers
Recursive vs. closed-form definition
Arithmetic and geometric sequences
Limit of a sequence

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students confuse the index n with the value a_n and cannot translate between recursive and closed forms.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tabulate the first several terms from each description and derive the closed form for geometric sequences explicitly.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students assume every sequence converges or that a limit is always attained by some term.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast convergent, divergent, and oscillating examples and connect to the upcoming limit definition.

Concept.name: The Limit Concept and Formal Definition
Concept.summary: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes the value f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a, independent of f(a). The formal epsilon-delta definition makes this precise and is used to prove basic limit laws.
key_definitions: Limit: lim_{x->a} f(x) = L means that for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < delta implies |f(x) - L| < epsilon.
One-sided limit: lim_{x->a^-} f(x) and lim_{x->a^+} f(x), approached from below and above a respectively.
Two-sided limit exists iff both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat the limit as simply f(a), plugging in a and concluding the limit exists even when f is undefined or discontinuous at a.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast examples where f(a) is undefined or differs from the limit (e.g., removable discontinuities) and require evaluating limits from tables and graphs before substitution.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students read the epsilon-delta definition as a procedure to compute limits rather than a condition to verify a candidate value.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Work small epsilon-delta proofs where the candidate L is given, emphasizing the quantifier order (for every epsilon there exists delta) with concrete numeric examples.

Concept.name: Continuity
Concept.summary: A function is continuous at a point when its limit there equals its value; continuity on an interval requires this at every interior point with appropriate one-sided conditions at endpoints. Discontinuities are classified as removable, jump, or infinite.
key_definitions: Continuity at a point: f is continuous at a if lim_{x->a} f(x) = f(a), which requires f(a) defined, the limit exists, and the two agree.
Removable discontinuity: the limit exists but does not equal f(a) (or f(a) is undefined).
Jump discontinuity: the one-sided limits exist but differ.
Infinite discontinuity: at least one one-sided limit is infinite.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students believe a function drawn without lifting the pen is automatically continuous everywhere, missing that continuity is a pointwise property and can fail at a single point.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Give piecewise-defined examples continuous on most of their domain but discontinuous at one point, and have students test the three continuity conditions at that point.

Concept.name: Limits at Infinity
Concept.summary: Limits at infinity describe the long-run behavior of a function, including horizontal asymptotes. The formal definition extends the epsilon-delta framework to x growing without bound.
key_definitions: Limit at infinity: lim_{x->infinity} f(x) = L means that for every epsilon > 0 there exists M such that x > M implies |f(x) - L| < epsilon.
Horizontal asymptote: the line y = L when lim_{x->infinity} f(x) = L or lim_{x->-infinity} f(x) = L.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students assume every function has a finite limit at infinity, or confuse a horizontal asymptote with a value the function actually reaches.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Compare rational functions of differing degrees, exponential growth versus decay, and oscillating functions, and stress that an asymptote describes approach, not attainment.

Concept.name: Trigonometric Limits and the Sandwich Theorem
Concept.summary: Special trigonometric limits such as lim_{x->0} sin(x)/x = 1 are established geometrically, and the Sandwich (Squeeze) Theorem is used to evaluate limits by bounding a function between two simpler ones with a common limit.
key_definitions: Sandwich Theorem: if g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) near a and lim_{x->a} g(x) = lim_{x->a} h(x) = L, then lim_{x->a} f(x) = L.
Fundamental trigonometric limit: lim_{x->0} sin(x)/x = 1 (with x in radians).

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the sin(x)/x result with x in degrees, or assume sin(x)/x -> 1 for any argument without matching the argument to the denominator.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Emphasize the radian requirement and practice variants such as sin(kx)/x by rewriting the expression to expose the matching argument.

Concept.name: Properties of Continuous Functions
Concept.summary: Continuous functions on closed intervals satisfy powerful existence theorems — the Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem — that guarantee roots and extrema without explicit computation.
key_definitions: Intermediate Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and k lies between f(a) and f(b), there exists c in (a, b) with f(c) = k.
Extreme Value Theorem: if f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then f attains both a maximum and a minimum on [a, b].

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students invoke the Intermediate Value Theorem to conclude a root exists without checking continuity on the closed interval, or apply the Extreme Value Theorem on an open interval.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require students to state the hypotheses explicitly before each application and provide counterexamples where a hypothesis fails and the conclusion breaks down.

Concept.name: Formal Definition of the Derivative
Concept.summary: The derivative of a function at a point is defined as the limit of the difference quotient as the increment in the input approaches zero; geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line, and physically or biologically it is an instantaneous rate of change.
key_definitions: Derivative at a point: f'(a) = lim_{h->0} [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h, provided the limit exists
Difference quotient: [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h, the average rate of change over an interval of length h
Differentiability at a point: the derivative exists as a finite limit at that point
Tangent line at a: the line through (a, f(a)) with slope f'(a)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat f'(a) as just 'plug a into a formula' and lose track of the fact that the derivative is itself a limit, so they cannot compute a derivative from the definition when no rule applies.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students compute difference quotients and take the limit explicitly for a polynomial and for 1/x before any shortcut rules are introduced, and require the limit notation in every step.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students assume every continuous function is differentiable, or that differentiability at a point is automatic from the graph looking smooth.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast |x| at 0 and a jump discontinuity with worked left- and right-hand difference-quotient limits, and have students classify given graphs as continuous-only, differentiable-only, or both.

Concept.name: Basic Rules of Derivatives
Concept.summary: Constant, constant-multiple, sum, and difference rules let derivatives of combinations of simple functions be computed term by term instead of from the limit definition each time.
key_definitions: Constant rule: d/dx[c] = 0
Constant-multiple rule: d/dx[c f(x)] = c f'(x)
Sum and difference rules: d/dx[f(x) ± g(x)] = f'(x) ± g'(x)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the sum rule to products, writing (fg)' = f'g', because the rules all look like 'differentiate each piece'.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Show a counterexample with explicit functions (e.g. f = g = x) where (fg)' ≠ f'g', and postpone product-rule work until students can state why the sum rule does not extend to products.

Concept.name: Power Rule and Rules of Differentiation
Concept.summary: The power rule gives d/dx[x^n] = n x^{n-1} for constant exponents, and together with the basic rules it makes polynomial and simple rational-power derivatives routine.
key_definitions: Power rule: d/dx[x^n] = n x^{n-1} for constant n
Rewriting before differentiating: expressing roots and reciprocals as powers so the power rule applies

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the power rule to expressions with the variable in the exponent, such as 2^x, treating the exponent as a constant multiplier.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students sort a mixed list of expressions into 'power rule applies' and 'power rule does not apply' before introducing exponential derivatives, and revisit the sort after Section 4.9.

Concept.name: Product and Quotient Rules
Concept.summary: The product rule and quotient rule give derivatives of products and ratios of differentiable functions in terms of the factors and their derivatives.
key_definitions: Product rule: d/dx[f(x) g(x)] = f'(x) g(x) + f(x) g'(x)
Quotient rule: d/dx[f(x)/g(x)] = [f'(x) g(x) - f(x) g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2, where g(x) ≠ 0

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students memorize the quotient rule with the terms in the wrong order or with the wrong sign, producing f'g - fg' over g^2 instead of fg' - f'g over g^2.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Anchor the quotient rule to the product rule by deriving it from f/g = f · g^{-1} with the chain rule, and have students re-derive it once before using it on problems.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students drop the second term of the product rule when one factor is a constant or when the product is written in an unfamiliar order.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require students to label f and g explicitly before differentiating, and include problems where the constant factor is written on either side.

Concept.name: The Chain Rule
Concept.summary: The chain rule differentiates compositions: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) g'(x), expressing the derivative of a composite as the outer derivative evaluated at the inner function times the inner derivative.
key_definitions: Chain rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) g'(x)
Inner and outer functions: the decomposition of a composite into g (inner) and f (outer)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students forget the inner derivative and write d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)), effectively treating the composition as a single function.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require an explicit decomposition step (name u = g(x), compute du/dx) on every chain-rule problem until students consistently include the inner factor.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students cannot identify the inner function when the composition is nested more than once, such as sin(cos(x^2)).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Practice peeling compositions from the outside in, writing the chain as a product of derivatives at each layer before simplifying.

Concept.name: Implicit Functions and Implicit Differentiation
Concept.summary: When a curve is given by an equation relating x and y rather than by y = f(x), implicit differentiation differentiates both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, and solves for dy/dx.
key_definitions: Implicit function: a relation F(x, y) = 0 that defines y locally as a function of x
Implicit differentiation: differentiating both sides of a relation with respect to x and applying the chain rule to terms involving y

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students differentiate y as if it were a constant, writing d/dx[y] = 0 instead of dy/dx.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students annotate every y-term with 'y is a function of x' and apply the chain rule explicitly to each y-term before solving for dy/dx.

Concept.name: Higher Derivatives
Concept.summary: Higher derivatives are obtained by differentiating repeatedly; the second derivative measures the rate of change of the first derivative and carries physical and biological meaning such as acceleration.
key_definitions: Second derivative: f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)]
nth derivative: f^{(n)}(x), the result of differentiating f n times
Notation: f'', f^{(n)}, d^2y/dx^2

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students interpret the second derivative as the square of the first derivative, or as (f')^2, rather than as the derivative of f'.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students compute f'' by first writing f' explicitly and then differentiating that expression, and contrast f'' with (f')^2 numerically for a sample function.

Concept.name: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
Concept.summary: The derivatives of sine and cosine follow from the limit definition together with the special trigonometric limits, and the remaining trigonometric derivatives follow by the quotient rule.
key_definitions: d/dx[sin x] = cos x and d/dx[cos x] = -sin x
Derivatives of tan, cot, sec, and csc obtained from the quotient rule

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students drop the negative sign in d/dx[cos x] = -sin x, or confuse the derivatives of sine and cosine.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Derive both derivatives from the limit definition once, and have students verify signs against the graphs of sine and cosine near zero.

Concept.name: Derivatives of Exponential Functions
Concept.summary: The exponential function e^x is its own derivative, and more generally d/dx[a^x] = a^x ln a; combined with the chain rule this differentiates exponential models of growth and decay.
key_definitions: d/dx[e^x] = e^x
d/dx[a^x] = a^x ln a for a > 0
The number e as the base for which the derivative of a^x equals a^x

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the power rule to exponentials, writing d/dx[2^x] = x 2^{x-1}.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Revisit the earlier sort of power-rule versus non-power-rule expressions, and derive d/dx[a^x] = a^x ln a from the limit definition so the ln a factor is not a memorized afterthought.

Concept.name: Derivatives of Inverse Functions
Concept.summary: If f is one-to-one and differentiable with nonzero derivative, its inverse is differentiable and (f^{-1})'(y) = 1 / f'(x) where y = f(x); this yields the derivatives of the logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions.
key_definitions: Inverse function derivative: (f^{-1})'(y) = 1 / f'(f^{-1}(y))
d/dx[ln x] = 1/x for x > 0
Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions obtained from the inverse-function rule

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students write the derivative of the inverse as the inverse of the derivative, i.e. (f^{-1})'(x) = 1/f'(x), without evaluating f' at the correct point.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Work through a table-based example where f(2) = 5 and f'(2) = 3, and have students compute (f^{-1})'(5) explicitly before generalizing.

Concept.name: Linear Approximation
Concept.summary: Near a point where f is differentiable, f can be approximated by its tangent line, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x - a); this linearization estimates function values and underlies the differential notation dy = f'(a) dx.
key_definitions: Linearization of f at a: L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)
Differential: dy = f'(a) dx, the change in the linear approximation corresponding to a change dx in x

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students use the linear approximation far from the base point and treat the estimate as exact, without checking that the approximation is only local.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students compare L(x) with f(x) at increasing distances from a and discuss where the error becomes unacceptable, tying the discussion to the tangent-line picture.

Concept.name: Extreme Value Theorem and Mean Value Theorem
Concept.summary: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval attains a maximum and minimum; the Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point where the instantaneous rate equals the average rate of change. Both underpin the later analysis of monotonicity, extrema, and optimization.
key_definitions: Absolute (global) maximum/minimum on an interval
Local (relative) extremum
Critical point: an interior point where f'(c)=0 or f'(c) does not exist
Extreme Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b], then f attains an absolute max and min on [a,b]
Mean Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there exists c in (a,b) with f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat the hypotheses of the Extreme Value Theorem and Mean Value Theorem as optional, applying them to functions that are discontinuous or to open intervals.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students construct counterexamples (e.g., f(x)=1/x on (0,1], or f(x)=|x| on [-1,1]) and identify exactly which hypothesis fails.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students believe the Mean Value Theorem identifies a unique point c, or that c must be a critical point.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use a sketch with a secant line and several parallel tangents to show c need not be unique and need not satisfy f'(c)=0.

Concept.name: Monotonicity and Concavity
Concept.summary: The sign of the first derivative determines where a function is increasing or decreasing, and the sign of the second derivative determines concavity. These sign analyses translate derivative information into a qualitative description of a function's graph.
key_definitions: Increasing/decreasing on an interval
Concave up / concave down
First-derivative test for monotonicity
Second-derivative test for concavity

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students conflate 'increasing' with 'positive' and 'decreasing' with 'negative', rather than reading the sign of the derivative.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Give sign-chart exercises where f is positive but decreasing, and require students to justify intervals using f' rather than f.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students assume a function is concave up wherever it is increasing.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast f(x)=x^2 on (0,∞) with f(x)=sqrt(x) on (0,∞) to separate first- and second-derivative information.

Concept.name: Extrema and Inflection Points
Concept.summary: Critical points and sign changes of the first derivative locate local extrema, while sign changes of the second derivative locate inflection points. Together with endpoint behavior, these produce a complete sketch of a function's graph.
key_definitions: Local maximum/minimum at a critical point
First-derivative test
Second-derivative test
Inflection point: a point where concavity changes

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat every critical point as an extremum, or every point with f''(x)=0 as an inflection point.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use f(x)=x^3 (critical point but no extremum) and f(x)=x^4 (f''(0)=0 but no inflection) as explicit counterexamples.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the second-derivative test when f''(c)=0 and conclude 'no extremum' rather than 'test inconclusive'.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require students to state the test's conclusion explicitly and fall back to the first-derivative test when f''(c)=0.

Concept.name: Optimization
Concept.summary: Optimization uses derivatives to find the largest or smallest value of a quantity subject to constraints, typically by expressing the quantity as a function of one variable, locating critical points, and verifying the extremum on the relevant interval.
key_definitions: Objective function
Constraint equation
Feasible interval
Closed-interval (candidate) method for absolute extrema

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students set the derivative to zero without first reducing the objective to a single variable using the constraint.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require an explicit 'constraint → substitution → single-variable objective' step before differentiating.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students report a critical point as the answer without checking endpoints or confirming it is a maximum/minimum on the feasible interval.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Insist on the closed-interval candidate method or a sign/concavity justification for every optimization answer.

Concept.name: L'Hôpital's Rule
Concept.summary: L'Hôpital's Rule evaluates limits of indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞ by replacing the ratio of functions with the ratio of their derivatives, and can be extended to other indeterminate forms after algebraic rewriting.
key_definitions: Indeterminate form 0/0 and ∞/∞
L'Hôpital's Rule statement and hypotheses
Other indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0) and their reductions

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply L'Hôpital's Rule to limits that are not indeterminate (e.g., 1/0 or 2/3).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require students to verify and label the indeterminate form before differentiating.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students differentiate the quotient as a whole (using the quotient rule) instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast d/dx[f/g] with f'/g' in a worked example and emphasize the rule replaces the ratio, not the quotient rule.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students stop after one application when the form is still indeterminate, or loop indefinitely without simplifying.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students re-check the form after each application and simplify algebraically between steps.

Concept.name: Antiderivatives
Concept.summary: An antiderivative of a function f is a function F whose derivative is f; the family of all antiderivatives differs by an additive constant, and basic antiderivative rules invert the differentiation rules.
key_definitions: Antiderivative: F is an antiderivative of f on an interval I if F'(x) = f(x) for all x in I.
Indefinite integral: ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C, the family of all antiderivatives of f.
Constant of integration: the arbitrary additive constant C distinguishing members of the antiderivative family.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students drop the constant of integration or treat ∫f(x)dx as a single function rather than a family of functions.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students verify antiderivatives by differentiating and show that two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant on an interval.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply the power rule for derivatives verbatim to antiderivatives, writing ∫x^n dx = n x^(n-1) instead of raising the exponent.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Derive the antiderivative power rule by differentiating x^(n+1)/(n+1) and contrast it side-by-side with the derivative power rule.

Concept.name: The Definite Integral
Concept.summary: The definite integral of a nonnegative function over an interval is the limit of Riemann sums and equals the area under the curve; it is defined via partitions, sample points, and the limit as the mesh goes to zero.
key_definitions: Riemann sum: Σ f(x_i*) Δx over a partition of [a,b] with sample points x_i*.
Definite integral: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = lim_{mesh→0} Σ f(x_i*) Δx, when the limit exists.
Integrable function: a function for which the Riemann-sum limit exists; continuous functions on [a,b] are integrable.
Signed area: the definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students conflate the definite integral with an antiderivative and expect ∫_a^b f(x) dx to be a function of x rather than a number.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Emphasize the definite integral as a limit of sums producing a real number, and compute simple integrals directly from Riemann sums before introducing the Fundamental Theorem.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students assume the integral always equals geometric area and ignore sign for functions that dip below the axis.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Work examples with sign changes and compare the Riemann-sum limit with the net signed area, distinguishing it from total area.

Concept.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Concept.summary: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links differentiation and integration: the integral function of a continuous f is an antiderivative of f, and the definite integral of f equals F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F.
key_definitions: Accumulation function: A(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt, whose derivative is f(x) when f is continuous.
FTC Part 1: If f is continuous on [a,b], then d/dx ∫_a^x f(t) dt = f(x).
FTC Part 2 (Evaluation Theorem): If F is any antiderivative of f on [a,b], then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students treat the two parts of the FTC as unrelated facts and cannot explain why differentiation and integration are inverse processes.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Derive Part 1 from the definition of the derivative of the accumulation function and use it to motivate Part 2, showing the inverse relationship explicitly.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students apply FTC Part 2 to functions that are not continuous on the interval or forget that F must be an antiderivative on the whole interval.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Include examples where continuity fails and require students to check hypotheses before evaluating.

Concept.name: Applications of Integration
Concept.summary: Definite integrals model accumulated change and geometric quantities, including net change from a rate, area between curves, and average value of a function, with applications drawn from biology and the social sciences.
key_definitions: Net change theorem: ∫_a^b F'(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), the integral of a rate of change gives total change.
Area between curves: ∫_a^b (f(x) − g(x)) dx for f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a,b].
Average value of f on [a,b]: (1/(b−a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students set up area-between-curves integrals without checking which curve is on top, producing sign errors.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require a sketch and an explicit comparison of f and g on the interval before writing the integral.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students cannot translate a word problem about a rate (e.g., population growth rate, marginal cost) into a definite integral of that rate.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Practice the net-change interpretation with concrete bio/social-science contexts, matching given units of the rate to units of the accumulated quantity.

Concept.name: The Substitution Rule
Concept.summary: The substitution rule (u-substitution) reverses the chain rule: by replacing an inner function with a new variable u, an integral of the form ∫ f(g(x))g'(x) dx becomes ∫ f(u) du, which is often elementary. For definite integrals the limits must be converted to u-values, or the antiderivative must be re-expressed in x before evaluating.
key_definitions: Substitution rule (u-substitution): ∫ f(g(x))g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du where u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx
Change of limits: for a definite integral, when u = g(x), the new limits are g(a) and g(b)
Differential: du = g'(x) dx, the formal device that converts the integrand and the differential together

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students substitute u = g(x) but leave the differential as dx, producing a mixed integral in both x and u.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require every substitution to be written as a pair (u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx) before any integration, and check that no x remains in the transformed integral.

difficulty_notes.misconception: On definite integrals students change the variable to u but keep the original x-limits, evaluating the u-antiderivative at x-values.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Insist on one of two explicit workflows: convert limits to u-values at the moment of substitution, or back-substitute to x before applying the original limits — never mix the two.

Concept.name: Integration by Parts
Concept.summary: Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. It converts an integral into a hopefully simpler one and is the standard tool for products of polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric factors, sometimes applied repeatedly.
key_definitions: Integration by parts formula: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du (indefinite) and ∫_a^b u dv = [uv]_a^b − ∫_a^b v du (definite)
Choice of u and dv: the assignment of factors in the integrand to u (to be differentiated) and dv (to be integrated)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students pick u and dv arbitrarily, producing a new integral ∫ v du that is harder than the original.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Teach a selection heuristic (e.g. choose u so that differentiating it simplifies it — logarithmic, inverse-trig, polynomial, exponential, trig in that priority) and have students predict whether ∫ v du is simpler before committing.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students forget the minus sign or drop the boundary term [uv]_a^b in the definite-integral version.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Have students write the full template ∫_a^b u dv = [uv]_a^b − ∫_a^b v du with the bracket explicitly before substituting any functions.

Concept.name: Rational Functions and Partial Fractions
Concept.summary: Rational functions P(x)/Q(x) with deg P < deg Q can be decomposed into a sum of simpler fractions whose denominators are the linear and irreducible quadratic factors of Q(x); each simple fraction is then integrated by standard rules (logarithms and arctangents). If deg P ≥ deg Q, polynomial long division is performed first.
key_definitions: Proper rational function: a rational function P(x)/Q(x) with deg P < deg Q
Partial fraction decomposition: writing a proper rational function as a sum of terms A/(x − r)^k and (Bx + C)/(x^2 + bx + c)^k corresponding to the factors of Q(x)
Repeated linear factor: a factor (x − r)^k requires terms A_1/(x − r) + … + A_k/(x − r)^k

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students attempt partial fractions on an improper rational function (deg P ≥ deg Q) without first dividing.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Make degree comparison the mandatory first step of every rational-integral problem, with long division performed whenever deg P ≥ deg Q.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students set up the decomposition with the wrong number of terms for repeated or irreducible quadratic factors (e.g. a single A/(x − r)^2 instead of A/(x − r) + B/(x − r)^2).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require students to fully factor Q(x) over the reals and write one term per power of each factor before solving for constants.

Concept.name: Practicing Integration: Choosing a Technique
Concept.summary: Given an arbitrary integral, the student must classify the integrand and select among substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, or a combination, sometimes applying techniques in sequence. This is the synthesis concept of the module: recognizing which tool applies rather than executing a prescribed one.
key_definitions: Integration strategy: an ordered decision procedure — simplify the integrand, look for an obvious substitution, classify as a product (parts) or rational function (partial fractions), and iterate

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students default to whichever technique was most recently taught regardless of the integrand's structure.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use mixed practice sets with no technique labels and require students to justify their choice of method in one sentence before integrating.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Students stop after one technique when a second is needed (e.g. a substitution followed by parts).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Assign multi-step problems explicitly and have students annotate each stage of the solution with the technique used.

LearningObjective.text: Determine the domain and range of a given function and identify its family (polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric).
Form compositions and inverses of functions and verify the inverse relationship by composition.
Explain how the shape and behavior of each standard function family will matter for limits and derivatives later in the course.
Model a growth or decay situation with N(t) = N0 e^{rt} and interpret N0 and r in context.
Convert between exponential forms and compute doubling time or half-life from the growth constant.
Evaluate the assumptions and limitations of an exponential model in a biological or social-science setting.
Describe a sequence by both a recursive and a closed-form rule and convert between the two for arithmetic and geometric cases.
Determine the limit of a simple sequence and classify it as convergent or divergent.
Explain how the limit of a sequence anticipates the limit of a function.
Explain in words what lim_{x->a} f(x) = L means and why the value of f(a) is irrelevant to the limit.
Apply the formal epsilon-delta definition to verify a stated limit for a simple linear or quadratic function.
Evaluate one-sided and two-sided limits from graphs, tables, and algebraic manipulation, determining when a limit fails to exist.
Determine whether a function is continuous at a point or on an interval by checking the continuity conditions.
Classify a given discontinuity as removable, jump, or infinite and justify the classification.
Evaluate limits at infinity for rational, exponential, and algebraic functions and identify horizontal asymptotes.
State the formal definition of a limit at infinity and use it to verify a simple long-run limit.
Derive or justify the limit lim_{x->0} sin(x)/x = 1 using a geometric argument.
Apply the Sandwich Theorem to evaluate limits by constructing appropriate bounding functions.
Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that an equation has a solution on a given interval.
Evaluate when the Extreme Value Theorem applies and explain why its hypotheses are necessary.
State the limit definition of the derivative at a point and explain each part of the difference quotient.
Compute the derivative of a given function at a point directly from the limit definition.
Determine from a graph or a piecewise formula whether a function is differentiable at a point, and relate differentiability to continuity.
State the constant, constant-multiple, sum, and difference rules for derivatives.
Differentiate polynomials and simple sums and differences using the basic rules.
State the power rule and identify the class of functions to which it applies.
Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers and differentiate them with the power rule.
State the product and quotient rules correctly, including the order of terms and signs.
Apply the product and quotient rules to differentiate products and ratios of polynomial, rational, and trigonometric functions.
Derive the quotient rule from the product rule and the chain rule.
State the chain rule and identify the inner and outer functions in a composite.
Differentiate composite functions, including nested compositions, using the chain rule.
Combine the chain rule with the product and quotient rules to differentiate complex expressions.
Explain why differentiating a term in y requires the chain rule when y is treated as a function of x.
Use implicit differentiation to find dy/dx for a curve given by an equation in x and y.
Compute second and higher derivatives of a given function.
Interpret the second derivative as the rate of change of the first derivative in a physical or biological context.
State the derivatives of sine and cosine and derive them from the limit definition using the special trigonometric limits.
Differentiate expressions involving trigonometric functions using the quotient rule and the chain rule.
State and justify that d/dx[e^x] = e^x and d/dx[a^x] = a^x ln a.
Differentiate exponential functions, including compositions with the chain rule.
Apply exponential derivatives to compute instantaneous rates of change in exponential growth and decay models.
State the inverse-function derivative formula and explain the condition under which it applies.
Use the inverse-function rule to compute derivatives of inverse functions, including ln x and inverse trigonometric functions.
Construct the linearization of a differentiable function at a point.
Use a linear approximation to estimate a function value and its change near a base point.
Evaluate the accuracy of a linear approximation and explain why it is only local.
State the Extreme Value Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem, including all hypotheses.
Explain why each hypothesis is necessary by constructing counterexamples when it fails.
Apply the Mean Value Theorem to find a point where the instantaneous rate equals the average rate of change on an interval.
Determine intervals of increase and decrease from the sign of the first derivative.
Determine intervals of concavity from the sign of the second derivative.
Construct a sign chart for f' and f'' and use it to describe the shape of a graph.
Classify critical points as local maxima, local minima, or neither using the first- and second-derivative tests.
Identify inflection points and explain their relationship to concavity changes.
Sketch the graph of a function using information from its first and second derivatives.
Translate a word problem into an objective function and a constraint.
Solve constrained optimization problems by reducing to one variable and locating extrema.
Justify that a candidate solution is a global extremum on the feasible interval, including endpoint checks.
Identify indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞ and state the hypotheses of L'Hôpital's Rule.
Apply L'Hôpital's Rule to evaluate limits of indeterminate form, including repeated applications.
Rewrite other indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0) into 0/0 or ∞/∞ and evaluate the limit.
Define an antiderivative and explain why antiderivatives of a function differ by an additive constant.
Compute indefinite integrals of power, polynomial, trigonometric, and exponential functions using basic antiderivative rules.
Verify a proposed antiderivative by differentiation and determine the constant from an initial condition.
Explain the definite integral as the limit of Riemann sums over partitions of an interval.
Approximate a definite integral using Riemann sums and interpret the result as signed area.
Evaluate definite integrals of simple functions directly from the definition.
State both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and explain how they show differentiation and integration are inverse processes.
Differentiate accumulation functions using FTC Part 1, including cases with a variable upper limit.
Evaluate definite integrals using FTC Part 2 and an antiderivative, checking the continuity hypotheses.
Apply the net change theorem to compute total change from a rate of change in biological and social-science contexts.
Set up and evaluate definite integrals for the area between two curves.
Compute the average value of a function on an interval and interpret it in context.
Explain how the substitution rule reverses the chain rule and state the rule for both indefinite and definite integrals.
Apply u-substitution to evaluate indefinite integrals, including choosing u and converting the differential.
Evaluate definite integrals by substitution, correctly converting the limits of integration.
Derive the integration-by-parts formula from the product rule and state it for indefinite and definite integrals.
Apply integration by parts to evaluate integrals involving products of polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions.
Evaluate integrals requiring repeated application of integration by parts and justify the choice of u and dv.
Explain the conditions under which a rational function admits a partial fraction decomposition and describe the form of the decomposition for linear, repeated, and irreducible quadratic factors.
Perform polynomial long division and partial fraction decomposition to rewrite a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions.
Integrate rational functions by decomposing them into partial fractions and evaluating the resulting elementary integrals.
Classify an integrand and select an appropriate integration technique, justifying the choice.
Evaluate integrals that require combining substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions in sequence.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Section 4.11 introduces the linearization L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a), the differential dy = f'(a) dx, and the use of tangent lines to estimate function values.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Extreme Value Theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval attains absolute maximum and minimum values. Mean Value Theorem: for f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), there is c in (a,b) with f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: A differentiable function is increasing where f'(x)>0 and decreasing where f'(x)<0; it is concave up where f''(x)>0 and concave down where f''(x)<0.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Local extrema occur at critical points and are classified by the first- or second-derivative test; inflection points are points where concavity changes, detected by sign changes of f''.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Optimization problems are solved by expressing the quantity to be optimized as a function of one variable using the constraint, then locating extrema on the feasible interval, including endpoints.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: L'Hôpital's Rule: if lim f(x)/g(x) is of indeterminate form 0/0 or ∞/∞, then under differentiability hypotheses the limit equals lim f'(x)/g'(x); other indeterminate forms are reduced to these by algebraic rewriting.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th Edition, Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Section 5.10 introduces antiderivatives and indefinite integrals, the constant of integration, and basic antiderivative rules obtained by inverting differentiation rules.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th Edition, Pearson, 2018.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th Edition, Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Section 6.2 presents both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the accumulation function, and evaluation of definite integrals via antiderivatives.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th Edition, Pearson, 2018.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.text_chunk: Section 7.1 introduces the substitution rule as the reverse of the chain rule, develops the change of variable u = g(x) with du = g'(x) dx, and treats definite integrals with converted limits.

Source.citation: Neuhauser, C. and Roper, M., Calculus for Biology and Medicine, 4th ed., Pearson, 2018.
Source.section: 7.2 Integration by Parts and Practicing Integration
